original_question: Does there exist an irreversible Finsler metric of finite volume on R x S^1 with no closed geodesics?
target_in_paper: Question 2.3.2 (Bangert) in §2.3, "Of complete Riemannian metrics with finite volume." ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already extremely close to the paper’s official formulation: it has the correct existence quantifier, the correct ambient manifold R × S^1, the irreversibility restriction, the finite-volume hypothesis, and the conclusion that there be no closed geodesics. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
missing_details: To make the question fully stand-alone, it helps to state explicitly that the manifold is the cylinder M = R × S^1.
It should define “irreversible” (nonreversible) rather than leaving that adjective implicit.
It should clarify that “closed geodesic” means a nonconstant periodic geodesic.

If one wants complete self-containment, one should say “finite total volume”; the statement in the paper itself says only “finite volume” and does not specify a particular Finsler-volume convention. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))

One should not add extra hypotheses such as completeness: although §2.3 is motivated by Question 2.3.1 on complete finite-volume Riemannian manifolds, Question 2.3.2 itself is stated without a completeness assumption. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
No ambient ring/field, degree restriction, homogeneity condition, nilpotency condition, or “for all sufficiently large m” quantifier is relevant to this geometric question.
refined_question: Does the cylinder M = R × S^1 admit an irreversible Finsler metric F (i.e. a nonreversible Finsler metric) of finite total volume such that F has no nonconstant closed geodesic? ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
justification: The draft is targeting Bangert’s exact open problem in §2.3 and is already nearly verbatim. The surrounding discussion explains the intended scope: the question is posed as the Finsler analogue of Question 2.3.1 on finite-volume Riemannian manifolds, after noting that reversible Finsler metrics are expected to behave similarly to the Riemannian case, whereas irreversible Finsler metrics can have only finitely many closed geodesics in compact examples. Therefore the sharp reformulation should keep precisely the cylinder R × S^1, the irreversibility condition, the finite-volume hypothesis, and the requirement of no closed geodesics, without broadening to other manifolds or silently adding completeness. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))

citations.label: Conjecture 2.2.1 and surrounding discussion on reversible vs. irreversible Finsler metrics
